item.title: Near-Future Strengthening of ENSO-Related Sea Ice Variability in We st Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Jihae Kim, Myong-In Lee, Daehyun Kang, Emilia Kyung Jin, Won Sang Lee, Seungseok Lee
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Antarctic, Antarctica, sea ice, model intercomparison
Abstract The increasing interannual variability of Antarctic sea ice near West Antarctica underscores the need to understand how El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnections may shape future sea ice changes. Using simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6, this study investigates the projected impacts of near-future ENSO variability on Antarctic sea ice. ENSO teleconnections are found to primarily influence Antarctic sea ice from austral winter through spring, and this influence is projected to strengthen in the near future. We show that the strengthened teleconnection is driven mainly by enhanced tropical forcing with the structural changes in tropical sea surface temperatures and precipitation, with a smaller contribution from changes in the midlatitude jet waveguide. These mechanisms are further supported by idealized nudging experiment using a dry dynamic core model. The strengthened teleconnection deepens the ENSO-induced mid-tropospheric circulation anomaly near West Antarctica, enhancing warm-air advection and the resulting sea ice anomalies. Overall, these changes are projected to increase Antarctic sea ice variability in the near future, highlighting the importance of understanding how evolving ENSO teleconnections may modulate Antarctic climate variability.

item.title: Reconstructing multi-temporal Glacier area changes to improve mass balance estimates in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau (2000–2025)
item.dc:creator: Zihao Li, Huan Xu, Wei Yang, Wenke Sun, Qiuyu Wang
item.description:
GIScience & Remote Sensing — matched: glacier, satellite altimetry, climate change
The southeastern Tibetan Plateau (SETP), a critical component of the “Asian Water Tower”, hosts a large concentration of maritime temperate glaciers that are highly sensitive to climate change. However, persistent cloud cover, seasonal snow, and supraglacial debris complicate consistent long-term glacier mapping, while the use of static glacier boundaries may introduce temporal mismatches in altimetry-based glacier mass-change estimates. In this study, we developed a multi-source data-fusion framework on Google Earth Engine (GEE) to reconstruct glacier-area changes in the SETP from 2000 to 2025 at five-year intervals and 30 m spatial resolution. Random Forest classifiers were used to integrate Landsat and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 synthetic-aperture-radar data, and NASADEM-derived topographic information, supporting glacier delineation under complex surface and atmospheric conditions. The reconstructed glacier area decreased from 8,083 ± 664 km2 in 2000 to 6,228 ± 572 km2 in 2025, corresponding to a cumulative loss of 22.9 ± 3.6% and a mean loss rate of 80.51 ± 10.51 km2 yr−1. The mean area-loss rates were 51.31 ± 6.51 km2 yr−1 during 2000–2010 and 92.99 ± 15.55 km2 yr−1 during 2010–2025, indicating a higher average loss rate in the later period. By combining satellite-altimetry-derived elevation changes from ICESat, CryoSat-2, and ICESat-2 with the reconstructed time-varying glacier areas, we estimated a mean glacier mass-change rate of −6.51 ± 1.22 Gt yr−1 during 2003–2022. Compared with using a fixed 2003 glacier area, the time-varying-area calculation reduced the estimated mass-loss magnitude by 0.63 Gt yr−1, equivalent to 8.8% of the fixed-area estimate. These results indicate that incorporating time-varying glacier areas can reduce temporal mismatch in altimetry-based mass-change estimation and improve the temporal consistency of regional glacier mass-change assessments.

item.title: Detecting Month-Dependent Predictability with Periodic Autoregressive Models: Reemergence and Predictability Barriers
item.dc:creator: Timothy DelSole, Martha Weaver Buckley, Michael K. Tippett
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: predictability, sea surface temperature
Abstract The climate system displays a seasonal cycle not only in its mean state, but also in predictability and variance. In particular, month-dependent autocorrelation functions (ACFs) reveal seasonal variations in persistence and are used routinely to characterize such phenomena as the spring predictability barrier in El Niño forecasts and the wintertime reemergence of sea surface temperature anomalies. However, detection of such behavior in climate data has often relied on heuristic procedures tailored to specific applications that are difficult to generalize to other applications. This paper proposes a general approach to detecting month-dependent ACFs based on Periodic Autoregressive (PAR) models, which extend standard autoregressive models by allowing parameters to vary with month. Specifically, a likelihood ratio test is used to determine if a PAR provides a significantly better fit than a stationary model with month-invariant parameters. Externally forced variability is incorporated through additional forcing terms. The resulting model provides a self-consistent representation of both internal and forced variability. Applying the test to observational records of sea surface temperature reveals distinct regions with statistically significant month-dependence in their ACFs. These include the tropical Pacific, where the method identifies the canonical spring predictability barrier, and several midlatitude regions displaying the statistical signature of reemergence. The test also identifies a previously undocumented seasonal rebound in the ACF over the Guinea Dome region of the northeastern tropical Atlantic. It is further shown that the widely used Seasonal Autoregressive (SAR) model cannot capture in a parsimonious manner the spring predictability barrier or reemergence.

item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: Antarctic, Antarctica
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) A 30-year dataset was made using infrared satellite data from November 1992–December 2022 to track the time, duration, and location of Cloud Mass Meridional Transport events (CMMTs). These events bring substantial heat and moisture poleward to Antarctica. CMMTs occurred more often during austral winter (JJA) and in regions such as Ellsworth Land in West Antarctica and Queen Maud Land in East Antarctica. The average number of CMMTs per year increased while their average duration decreased.

item.title: Hybrid ensemble forecasting combining physics-based and machine-learning predictions through spectral nudging
item.dc:creator: Inna Polichtchouk, Simon Lang, Sarah-Jane Lock, Michael Maier-Gerber, Peter Dueben
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ensemble, machine learning
arXiv:2603.05570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the first application of spectral nudging in a probabilistic ensemble forecasting framework, combining the physics-based ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System ensemble (IFS-ENS) with forecasts from the probabilistic machine-learned AIFS-ENS ensemble. Large scales of virtual temperature and vorticity are relaxed toward the machine-learned forecasts, while mesoscale structures remain governed by the physics-based model. This hybrid ensemble shows substantial improvements in large-scale forecast skill, with gains in predictive skill extended by up to two days in the tropics and by approximately half a day in the extra-tropics relative to IFS-ENS. Despite nudging being applied only to upper-air fields, improvements are also found in several near-surface parameters. Tropical cyclone track forecasts improve significantly, consistent with improved representation of the large-scale steering flow, without degrading storm intensity or ensemble spread. These results demonstrate that spectral nudging can be successfully extended to ensemble prediction and provide an attractive pathway for combining machine-learned and physics-based weather prediction systems.

item.title: Forecasting carbon-risk hotspots ahead of the extreme 2026 El Ni\~no
item.dc:creator: Xiaomeng Du, Runda Jiang, Philippe Ciais, Pierre Friedlingstein, Stephen Sitch, Mike O'Sullivan, … (+11)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: carbon cycle, ensemble, machine learning
arXiv:2610.16714v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A potentially super El Ni\~no is forecasted in 2026, raising the need to anticipate land carbon-cycle risks before its impacts unfold. We develop a prospective early-warning framework that uses dynamic global vegetation models driven by an ensemble of ECMWF seasonal climate forecasts and machine-learning burned area predictions. Forecasts indicate a $0.23 \pm 0.21$ PgC reduction in global net biome productivity in the second half of 2026, with hotspots of sink weakening in eastern South America and elevated fire risk in Southeast Asia.

item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: Antarctica, polar
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) We developed a new high-resolution global gravity field model by integrating satellite, marine, terrestrial, airborne, polar, and topographic gravity information. The model substantially improves gravity estimation accuracy in coastal, polar, and data-sparse regions. Accuracy improves by 9 %–24 % within 10 km of the coastline and by approximately 40 % over Antarctica. The dataset can be used for geodesy, oceanography, and other Earth science applications.

item.title: Optimization of the fast layer transmittance algorithm in RTTOV v13.1 for strong water vapor absorption channels of the FY-3F HIRAS-II instrument using LBLRTM v12.11
item.dc:creator: Panxiang Zhang, Peng Zhang, Gang Ma, Rui Li, Lu Lee, Wenguang Bai, … (+1)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
To enhance atmospheric transmittance accuracy in strong water vapor absorption bands, this study proposes an optimized scheme for the fast transmittance algorithm applied to the Hyperspectral Infrared Atmospheric Sounder-II. It introduces a transmittance threshold for sample selection and a weighted least squares regression with transmittance weighting. Validation against line-by-line models and observations shows significant improvements in forward model accuracy and stability at 6.7 μm.

item.title: A preliminary study on a synergistic assimilation scheme for multi-band satellite soil moisture data
item.dc:creator: Xuesong Bai, Zhaohui Lin, Zhengkun Qin, Juan Li
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Accurate soil moisture data is essential for predicting weather. This study examined how observations from three satellites can be combined to improve land-surface simulations. While each satellite helps, their value changes with vegetation type. Merging these data sources gives a more reliable estimate of soil wetness, especially in central and western China. This approach strengthens soil-water monitoring and supports more dependable climate forecasting.
